top.title: Yilwatda charges North-Central APC leaders to unite for Tinubu

In Benue State, he called on the governor and party leaders to harmonise competing interests, bring political stakeholders together and mobilise voters for the party. top.title: Ella Swindle to leave Texas volleyball; Jerritt Elliot emotional about setter's departure
top.description: Texas Longhorns setter Ella Swindle (1) celebrates a score during the NCAA Regional Final volleyball match against Wisconsin at Gregory Gym on Sunday, Dec. 14, 2025 in Austin. Martinez/Austin American-Statesman) Ella Swindle could have up to 10 more games in a Texas volleyball uniform, but Friday's sweep of Ole Miss served as a farewell of sorts for the star-crossed setter, who won't play for the Longhorns in her fifth and final collegiate season in 2027. After an emotional postgame senior night celebration that included rounds of hugs and even more tears, Swindle confirmed to reporters after the match that she plans to leave Texas (14-8, 10-4 SEC) following this year, which continues Sunday against LSU in the regular-season finale. The Texas Longhorns celebrate beating Texas A&M in the Lone Star Showdown volleyball match at Gregory Gym on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026 in Austin. (Aaron E. Martinez/Austin American-Statesman) "I'm definitely not done with volleyball," she said. "I'm kind of figuring things out. I think I'll know for sure in the next week or so. But I'm just praying about it a lot, and I know there's a really great plan in store. I've just been where my feet are and focusing on the moment that I'm in, but I'm definitely getting excited for what's next." Swindle's departure comes as no surprise, especially after fellow 2023 recruiting class members Torrey Stafford , Nya Bunton and Ramsey Gary announced their decision earlier this week to return to Texas for the 2027 season. Swindle and defensive specialist Anja Kujundžić were not a part of that announcement even though both four-year players still have one remaining year of eligibility. Both partook in Friday's senior night celebration. Setter in and out of rotation since freshman season By now, most Longhorn fans understand Swindle's saga. She helped lead Texas to a second consecutive national championship while earning freshman All-American honors in 2023, when she started all 32 matches and playing in all 114 sets. During her lone season as the full-time setter, Swindle amassed 1,088 assists, 227 digs and 92 blocks. But that season proved a high mark for Swindle at Texas. She served as the second setter to Averi Carlson as a sophomore before regaining the starting job last season. This year, she fell behind starter Rella Binney and freshman Genevieve Harris in the rotation and has only appeared in 10 matches. Prior to an emotional homecoming in the Longhorns' win Nov. 6 in Swindle's hometown of Columbia, Mo., Swindle had gone more than a month without seeing the court. Texas coach Jerritt Elliott has treaded lightly over the past few seasons when discussing his decisions at the setter position. top.description: 🔥 In-demand Antonio Nusa continues post-World Cup form for Norway Norway's resurgence on the European stage at both the club and international level has been something brilliant for Nordic football. Though Erling Haaland will undoubtedly continue to receive the attention he so richly deserves, and much of the same can be said of captain Martin Ødegaard, the supporting cast for Ståle Solbakken's Røde, Hvite, Blå deserves plenty of praise. Antonio Nusa, perhaps, more than any other. Still just 21, the RB Leipzig starlet has been in some of the finest form of his career after a very credible summer with Norway at the 2026 World Cup. That hot streak continued this evening in Oslo when he opened the scoring in Norway's Nations League A home clash against Wales, meaning Nusa has now found the back of the net or collected an assist in six-straight matches for club and country since his brace of helpers against Elversberg back on 24 October. Taking up his position on the left flank, Nusa did well to beat veteran shot-stopper Karl Darlow with a low drive from the top of the 18-yard box to break the deadlock after the half-time interval. It was Nusa's 10th goal for Norway, and the first for his country since the pair he bagged over the summer across the Atlantic. His pace outwide, competence on the ball, and ability to drive play forward at speed have been at the forefront of Norway's rekindling efforts, and perhaps it's no wonder that Premier League holders and current table-toppers Arsenal have recently been heavily linked with the former Club Brugge standout. Having started alongside the aforementioned Haaland and Ødegaard, as well as Fulham's Oscar Bobb tonight, will Nusa add his name to Norway's Premier League-based ranks come the opening of the January window?

top.title: 'I was envious': R Ashwin makes honest confession about Ravindra Jadeja
top.description: Ravichandran Ashwin has offered an interesting account of what made his bowling partnership with Ravindra Jadeja so successful, revealing how he learned to use the left-arm spinner's strengths and limitations to his advantage. Ashwin described Jadeja as an exceptionally gifted cricketer but suggested that the all-rounder initially lacked the instinct to consistently find ways to dismiss batters. The two formed one of the most successful spin combinations in Test cricket, sharing the field in 58 matches and accounting for 587 wickets. While Ashwin claimed 317 of those dismissals, Jadeja contributed 270. According to the former India off-spinner, their success stemmed from understanding each other's contrasting approaches and making the most of them. Speaking on Aakash Chopra's podcast show, Baith & Bol, Ashwin explained that he understood Jadeja's game well enough to help him operate within his strengths rather than push him towards something that did not come naturally to him. “I know his limitations well," Ashwin said. “Very few can bring him out of those limitations. I was one of them. His biggest strength: naturally gifted. If he has a bad day, you just tell him your effort is fine; tomorrow will be better. His action was simple, release point simple, tappa so good—he doesn’t have to think. He didn’t know how to dismiss batsmen—I’m saying he absolutely didn’t know. But his skill to choke batsmen was intertwined with his skill. You can’t sweep him—trajectory is low. You can’t step out—airspeed is good. You can’t play defense without doubting if the ball would remain the same." One aspect of Jadeja's bowling that often came under scrutiny was his reluctance to vary his pace or give the ball more flight, even when the conditions called for it. Ashwin revealed that he had attempted to persuade his spin partner to experiment more, but those efforts often came at the expense of Jadeja's effectiveness and economy. Eventually, Ashwin recognised that Jadeja's ability to keep things tight from one end gave him the freedom to attack from the other. While Jadeja restricted the opposition's scoring opportunities, Ashwin could experiment with different deliveries and concentrate on taking wickets. That combination also made Jadeja more difficult to deal with. Ashwin said developing this understanding gave him even greater appreciation for what Jadeja brought to the team, particularly his remarkable consistency and control. “When I understood that, my respect for Jadeja doubled—what he does is not easy. I have seen many skillful spinners, but the repetitive nature- keeping the ball there at the same speed is very difficult. Spinning the ball at that speed is not easy," he said. top.title: 'We've waited 73 years to be here' - Wales fans ecstatic after win over New Zealand
top.description: Saturday marked the first time Wales had beaten New Zealand in 73 years [Getty Images] Welsh rugby fans were "fizzing off their heads" on Saturday night after ending 73 years of hurt against New Zealand in an epic Nations Championship encounter. The match at the Principality Stadium ended 35-28 to the hosts as the All Blacks' run of 34 successive victories against Wales - dating back to 1953 - came to a juddering halt in Cardiff. Wales fans were left stunned by a result that came just a week on from having to grind out a win against Japan. Celebrities were also quick to congratulate the team with Gavin & Stacey star Ruth Jones sharing her disbelief in an Instagram post. Three times Wales led by 14 points, and for the first time in history they scored five tries against New Zealand, but ultimately it was heroic defensive work that denied the visitors. All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie made eight changes from the side that swept past Scotland in their previous Nations Championship game. But the approach backfired spectacularly after a brilliant performance sparked astonishing scenes in Cardiff. Darren Williams went to Caernarfon Rugby Club to watch the match [BBC] Darren Williams lives abroad but comes home once a year to visit his family in Wales. He came to Caernarfon Rugby Club to watch the match and said the result was "excellent". "I hope they can continue like this and keep moving forward," he said. "The atmosphere was excellent and very enthusiastic." Daron Owens said she was "really glad" to be at the rugby club to witness such a brilliant performance. "It was great to see everyone so proud. Everyone was cheering so loudly, it was a really positive place to be." One fan pitch side at Principality Stadium said they had waited "73 years to be at this game", adding that they were in "total shock but absolutely delighted". Daron Owens said everyone at the rugby club was "ecstatic" after the game [BBC] Celebrities and politicians were also quick to pay tribute to the team for their heroics on the field. Gavin and Stacey star Jones shared her sheer delight in an Instagram video, with the actor looked visibly stunned following the incredible win over New Zealand. Welsh politicians have also come forward to congratulate the team, including First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth. "This has been decades in the making. Huge congratulations to you all," he wrote on Facebook. "You should all be proud." Secretary of State for Wales Stephen Kinnock said he managed to watch the final part of the game after speaking at the Welsh Labour conference in Llandudno. "After 73 years we've finally beaten the All Blacks! Can barely believe what I've just witnessed," he said. top.description: Dewi Lake and Jac Morgan were the Wales co-captains at the 2023 World Cup in France [Huw Evans Picture Agency] Captain Dewi Lake says he always believed Wales could defeat New Zealand and end the 73-year hoodoo against the All Blacks. Wales never trailed in the 35-28 victory as they produced a magnificent display to beat New Zealand for the first time since 1953. Wales had lost the previous 34 matches in the fixture and had odds of 20-1 with the bookmakers before this game. But Lake says the group thought they could win. "Of course we did," said Lake. "Sometimes we sit in front of the media and say we can beat them and it's probably a passing comment for some media outlets or people at home. "It's not for us. We work hard, we have tough conversations, not only players, but coaches and staff. "There is much hard work that goes on for this group to grow and succeed. "For it to finally come to fruition and see it on the field makes me so proud." This is a special group - Tandy Lake's sentiments were echoed by head coach Tandy, who said he felt emotional after the win. "You could see what it means for the the players, nation and supporters," said Tandy. "It's incredible. We've been wanting some positivity and the players delivered that. "The overriding emotion is pride for the playing group, the staff and I'm just glad for everyone who represents Wales. "You always have belief. History tells you something different but I believe in the group. "They are a special group of people and I can't wait to come in every Monday to work with them." top.title: All Blacks ran into a Welsh brick wall - Barrett
top.description: Beauden Barrett won his 149th New Zealand cap against Wales [Press Association] Beauden Barrett said it felt like New Zealand were running into a red brick wall after they became the first All Blacks side to lose to Wales since 1953. Steve Tandy's men created history with a 35-28 victory at Principality Stadium thanks to a stirring defensive effort. Wales scored five tries - a national record against New Zealand - but it was their effort without the ball that ended a 34-game losing streak against the All Blacks. The home side made 346 tackles, with lock Dafydd Jenkins topping the chart with 38, and held the New Zealanders up over the line three times in the second half to protect their seven-point lead. "It felt like a brick wall at times, so you have to give them credit," said full-back Barrett, who captained New Zealand in a Test for the first time. "You give opportunities for the crowd to come into the game, and we are well aware of that when we come here. "That's why it's one of the best places to play rugby - it feels like you are playing 16 or 17." Magnificent Wales end 73-year New Zealand hoodoo Wales believed they could create history - Lake As it happened: Wales claim first win over New Zealand since 1953 Dave Rennie claimed an unwanted piece of history as the first All Blacks coach to lose to Wales in 73 years. The former Glasgow boss admitted New Zealand "certainly got out-passioned" but had no regrets about his selection. The All Blacks made eight changes to their starting line-up between their win against Scotland and their trip to England in the final Nations Championship group game. "We had a good enough side on the field to win, and if you look at the stats, we had plenty of opportunities and the guys created a lot of chances," said Rennie. "We just weren't clinical enough, and they were very good defensively. "I have no regret around the side that we picked, as I've talked about previously, there is really good competition for places. "There's not a lot between certain positions." Beaten All Blacks climb above Springboks Eddie James started alongside Max Llewellyn for the second time for Wales [Press Association] New Zealand still inched above South Africa, who lost a thriller in France on Friday, into top spot in the southern hemisphere table. If the All Blacks win with a bonus point at Twickenham on Saturday (14:10 GMT), they will secure top spot before the Springboks' game in Ireland (20:10 GMT). "It hurts, but you've got to take it on the chin," said Rennie, who took over from Scott Robertson at the start of the year. "We weren't good enough; Wales were passionate and every time they kept us out, they grew and became harder to break down. "We've got to be better, we expect a lot more of ourselves, and I need to see a response at Twickenham."

top.title: Eagles’ Howie Roseman Turns Heads With Darian Mensah Interaction
top.description: Philadelphia Eagles general manager Howie Roseman was in town to watch Miami standout quarterback Darian Mensah in person this week as the Hurricanes take on Duke. What makes that such a storyline? Well, the Eagles are facing an uncertain future with current franchise quarterback Jalen Hurts. Hurts was forced to end his season early due to multiple issues with blood clots. Hurts is facing an uncertain future himself. There are some who believe that he is facing an uphill battle to play football again. If the blood clot issues persist, he will need to stay on blood thinners, which would effectively end his ability to play football. Of course, all of that is pure speculation. No one truly knows what the future has in store for Hurts in Philadelphia. With that being said, if the Eagles do end up needing another quarterback, Roseman could target one in the 2027 NFL Draft. Mensah has been one of the most productive quarterbacks in college football this season. top.title: Why Urban Meyer is buying in to 24-team CFP expansion
top.description: Jerome Miron-Imagn Images Why Urban Meyer is buying in to 24-team CFP expansion appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . With the NCAA football landscape changing year-by-year, many fans and commentators have strong opinions about this shifting landscape. One of those changes is that the College Football Playoff will soon expand to 24 teams. Former college football coach Urban Meyer is okay with that . “My instant reaction is it’s not death if you lose,” Meyer said, per FOX. “…..Now you’re 12, and now 24. 24 if you lose, keep rolling.” The 24-team CFP is starting in 2027 and @CoachUrbanMeyer gives his thoughts pic.twitter.com/Eu5VyhoQHj Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) — Big Noon Kickoff (@BNKonFOX) November 14, 2026 The CFP format has moved from four teams to now 12 teams. The field will expand again to 24 teams, starting in 2027. That certainly allows more programs an opportunity to compete for a national championship . “The 24-team field will be made up of four guaranteed spots for Power 4 conference champions (ACC, Big Ten, Big 12 and SEC), one guaranteed spot for the highest-ranked team from the Group of 6 leagues (American, Conference USA, MAC, Mountain West, Pac-12 and Sun Belt) and 19 at-large spots chosen by the selection committee. Seeds 1-8 will earn a first-round bye and host a second-round game on campus. Seeds 9-24 will play first-round games on the campus of the higher seed,” The Athletic reported about the expansion. Due to the playoff expanding, there are also changes coming to scheduling rules for power 4 college football teams. In order to qualify for a spot in the expanded playoff, those teams will have to play at least 10 other power 4 schools each year. That includes conference opponents, and then teams from other power 4 leagues or Notre Dame. It appears that this latest expansion might be the last new change for a while with the CFP. “A move to a 24-team field in 2027 will mark five consecutive years with a change to the Playoff’s layout or format, but with this latest deal, talk of expansion is off the table for the near future,” The Athletic reported. top.title: Avalanche Lose MacKinnon for Extended Time, Makar for Two Weeks
top.description: USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Connect The Colorado Avalanche will be without superstars Nathan MacKinnon and Cale Makar for an extended period. Avalanche head coach Jared Bednar told reporters in Montreal on Saturday morning that MacKinnon is out for at least a month, while Makar is expected to miss two weeks. Both players suffered lower-body injuries in Ottawa, with the incidents occurring around a minute apart in the second period. To replace MacKinnon in the lineup , Colorado recalled forward Gavin Brindley from the American Hockey League on Saturday. The Denver Post’s Corey Masisak confirmed that Brock Nelson will move up to the top line in MacKinnon’s absence, while Nic Roy will center a line with Gabe Landeskog . Nazem Kadri will center another line. On defense, rookie Alex Gagne will make his NHL debut alongside Brent Burns, who is set to appear in his 1,600th career regular-season game. That likely means Noah Juulsen moves up to play with Brett Kulak, leaving Devon Toews and Sam Malinski together as the top pair. The top power play will also have Toews and Artturi Lehkonen on it. They’ll join Martin Necas, T.J. Hughes, and Kadri, as they did after Thursday’s injuries . MacKinnon is Colorado’s top point producer, recording 10 goals, 20 assists, and 30 points in 20 games this season. Makar, who previously missed a game for the birth of his twin children, has five goals and 23 points in 19 games. This is a rare situation for Colorado. Saturday’s matchup against the Canadiens will mark just the seventh time that both superstars have been unavailable for the same game since Makar made his NHL debut. It’s also the first time since March 2021 that both players will miss the same game outside of occasional late-season rest ahead of the playoffs. Bednar said Makar’s injury is soft tissue-related and that there is no concern it will linger beyond the current recovery timeline. The timing offers the Avalanche at least a little relief. Colorado has just five games scheduled over the next two weeks, meaning Makar could miss a relatively small portion of the schedule if he returns as expected. MacKinnon’s absence, however, is expected to stretch considerably longer. There’s no question that it’s going to be a challenge. nigeria.title: Spain will host 2030 World Cup final, federation president insists
nigeria.description: The 2030 World Cup final will be in Spain, Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) head Rafael Louzan reiterated on Saturday, adding that he is not considering “withdrawing” should he be wrong. Spain is organising the next World Cup with Portugal and Morocco. The decision on the venue for the final will be made in 2028, Louzan said. Spain favours Real Madrid’s Santiago Bernabeu Stadium for the final. Portugal does not have a suitable stadium but Morocco has suggested the 115,000-capacity Hassan II Stadium being built in Benslimane near Casablanca. “There is no other plan than for the final to be held in Spain,” said Louzan at a conference at the RFEF’s Ciudad del Futbol on the outskirts of Madrid. “I am not currently considering the possibility of withdrawing from Spain, as the prospect of Spain not hosting the final is not on the table,” he said. Louzan was responding to Alberto Nunez Feijoo, the leader of the right-wing People’s Party. In a television interview on November 5, Feijoo said that were he to become prime minister in the general election on November 29, he would advocate withdrawing Spain’s bid to host the World Cup should Morocco be awarded the final. Luzon said the question was entirely hypothetical. “That notion simply doesn’t exist,” he said, adding that under FIFA’s tradition of rotating the World Cup the staging of the final “belongs to the European continent”. A delegation of FIFA technical experts spent last week visiting Spanish stadiums that are hoping to host matches during the tournament, Louzan said. nigeria.title: FG raises alarm over 2,000 universities, 100 fake professors report
nigeria.description: By Joseph Erunke, ABUJA The Federal Government has dismissed viral claims that Nigeria has 2,000 universities and that about 100 professors in the country were exposed as fake, describing the reports as fabricated misinformation aimed at eroding public confidence in the nation’s university system. The government, through the Federal Ministry of Education, said the National Universities Commission, NUC, never made such declarations, published the alleged list of fake professors or authenticated the names currently circulating on social media. Minister of Education, Dr. Tunji Alausa, made the clarification in a statement issued on Saturday through the ministry’s Director of Press and Public Relations, Boriowo Folasade. He said the claims were false, misleading and a recycled version of old information being distorted to deceive the public. The ministry specifically faulted reports suggesting that the NUC had identified about 100 individuals as fake professors, explaining that the allegation was a misrepresentation of a media report published on December 3, 2019. According to the ministry, the original report concerned an exercise by the NUC to verify the directory of full professors in Nigerian universities and did not contain the names now being circulated online. It stressed that the commission had since disowned the purported list, insisting that it neither originated from the regulatory agency nor enjoyed its endorsement. 2,000 varsities On the claim that Nigeria has 2,000 universities, the ministry said the NUC had never announced the existence of such a number of universities in the country. The government expressed concern over what it described as the persistent recycling of false information, warning that such claims could undermine the credibility of Nigerian universities and damage efforts to strengthen standards in the nation’s higher education system. It urged media organisations, social media users and members of the public to exercise caution before sharing unverified information, particularly on issues concerning the recognition of universities and the integrity of academic qualifications. The ministry advised Nigerians to rely on the NUC’s official communication channels for accurate information on recognised universities, academic standards and regulatory decisions. It reaffirmed the Federal Government’s commitment to supporting the NUC in protecting academic integrity, strengthening quality assurance and preserving the credibility and international reputation of Nigeria’s university education system. Unfortunately, when she called, I couldn’t talk on the phone as I had been ambushed by my kids, who were brandishing their homework and threatening to cry if I didn’t help them. As a mom herself, she immediately understood why I couldn’t continue with the conversation. I quickly made my excuses, and we laughed and hung up, promising to catch up at a more convenient time. However, that exchange got me thinking about how most millennial women have a radically different marriage and motherhood timeline from our mothers. You see, when my mother was in her early 40s, my siblings and I were in university, so she had a lot of free time during the week to spend relaxing, hanging out with her friends, and attending social events. Basically living her best life. I, on the other hand, at 40-plus, spend my days cooking pot after pot of hot meals that immediately get devoured by my ever-hungry kids, teaching my nursery school-aged kids how to count and spell, and trying but often failing to enforce a strict bedtime with yelling and threats. I constantly feel myself going underwater and have to fight for my life every single day. There are other ways motherhood has been such a hugely different experience for me than it was for my mother. Like many women of her generation, she got married right after secondary school as university education was not seen as vital. This meant that she was a teenage mother and so had more energy to spare on her kids. She also benefited from having a lot of support from domestic staff and relatives. I do not have any village supporting me with child-rearing. I have hired domestic staff in the past, but it was always one thing or another, and they ended up leaving me stranded. I also do not have youth on my side, and I have the back pain and other aches to prove it. But this experience is not unique to me. Statistics show that most women globally will have their first child at 30 or 31, and we are seeing a lot more women becoming first-time moms at 35 and above. This is considered advanced maternal age. The fact is that as women increasingly prioritise university education and career stability before marriage, maternal age will continue to rise. This is not a trend that can be reversed. The wobbly Nigerian economy doesn’t help matters either, as people are putting off marriage till they can grow their finances, leading to advanced marital age across both genders. For instance, I have several male ex-classmates in their 40s who have given up on getting married because they cannot afford to. This is very unfortunate. entertainment.description: The Nigerian thriller series, directed by Wande Thomas and produced by Isoken Ogiemwonyi, is set to join KAVA’s growing slate of premium African content. Nigerian streaming platform KAVA is set to bring the psychological thriller series Spiraling , starring Toni Tones ( King of Boys ) and Jim Iyke , to audiences across its streaming service. Set against the high-stakes worlds of technology, power and politics in contemporary Nigeria, Spiraling follows Sade ( Toni Tones ), a brilliant tech entrepreneur whose carefully constructed life begins to unravel after an impulsive affair triggers a dangerous chain of events. Spiraling explores the darker side of ambition and the lengths people will go to protect their carefully constructed lives. Alongside Tones and Iyke, the ensemble cast includes Folu Storms , Seun Ajayi , Fae Olumide , Fiyinfoluwa Asenuga and Mathilda Akatugba . Created and directed by Wande Thomas ( Under the Influence , The Smart Money Woman ), the series is co-written by Thomas and Amaka Anioji and produced by Isoken Ogiemwonyi ( The Smart Money Woman , Ci ) . Director and creator Wande Thomas added: I wanted to explore how quickly an ordinary decision can spiral into something completely beyond your control. At its heart, this is a story about the secrets we keep, the lies we tell ourselves and how far we’ll go when everything is at stake. I’m excited for audiences to finally experience it. F Taofeeq/Spiraling Producer Isoken Ogiemwonyi said: With Spiraling , we wanted to take a simple story and tell it really well. We spent a lot of time developing the characters and exploring the darker side of very human emotions, ambition, desire and jealousy. entertainment.title: “Lagos Gave Me My Greatest Successes and Deepest Heartbreak”: DJ Cuppy Opens Up in Ifeoluwa Documentary
entertainment.description: Nigerian DJ and philanthropist Florence Otedola, popularly known as Cuppy, pictured wearing gold headphones and a camel-brown blazer. On her birthday, Florence Ifeoluwa Otedola is giving viewers a more personal glimpse into her life, exploring home, family, identity and purpose. For years, Nigerians have known Florence “Cuppy” Otedola as the internationally recognised DJ and philanthropist, often recognised by her signature pink hair and vibrant public personality. This birthday, however, her new documentary offers a closer look at the woman behind that familiar public image. Released on 11 November 2026, her new 12-minute documentary, Ifeoluwa , follows Cuppy back to Lagos, the city that shaped her and remains close to her heart. It is also a place connected to some of her greatest successes and deepest heartbreak. The title Ifeoluwa means “The Love of God”. Rather than marking the occasion with another glamorous birthday celebration, Cuppy has chosen to share a more reflective portrait of her life. The film explores womanhood, ambition, identity, belonging and the ongoing process of becoming. There are tender moments, too. Viewers see Cuppy not just as a public figure, but as a daughter, sister and granddaughter. Her time with her grandmother offers an especially intimate glimpse into the affection and family ties at the heart of her story. The documentary also captures an evolution audiences may already have noticed. Her signature pink hair has given way to a new look, while faith, education and service have become increasingly central to how Cuppy speaks about her future. This is not a rejection of music, but a fuller picture of the person behind it. Her philanthropic work remains an important part of that picture. Through the Cuppy Foundation, she has helped raise more than $17 million to support displaced children in Nigeria, in partnership with Save the Children. She has also established education funds at the University of Oxford, New York University and King’s College London to help students overcome financial barriers, particularly those from Africa. Alongside this work, Cuppy remains active as an international DJ, with performances at Glastonbury, Wireless Festival and Cannes Lions, as well as events during United Nations General Assembly week. At its heart, Ifeoluwa is a personal homecoming that brings together family, faith, Lagos and the experiences shaping Cuppy’s next chapter. It offers viewers a chance to see beyond the familiar celebrity image and learn more about the person behind it. Swindle's departure comes as no surprise, especially after fellow 2023 recruiting class members Torrey Stafford , Nya Bunton and Ramsey Gary announced their decision earlier this week to return to Texas for the 2027 season. Swindle and defensive specialist Anja Kujundžić were not a part of that announcement even though both four-year players still have one remaining year of eligibility. sports.description: 🔥 In-demand Antonio Nusa continues post-World Cup form for Norway Norway's resurgence on the European stage at both the club and international level has been something brilliant for Nordic football. Though Erling Haaland will undoubtedly continue to receive the attention he so richly deserves, and much of the same can be said of captain Martin Ødegaard, the supporting cast for Ståle Solbakken's Røde, Hvite, Blå deserves plenty of praise. Antonio Nusa, perhaps, more than any other. Still just 21, the RB Leipzig starlet has been in some of the finest form of his career after a very credible summer with Norway at the 2026 World Cup. That hot streak continued this evening in Oslo when he opened the scoring in Norway's Nations League A home clash against Wales, meaning Nusa has now found the back of the net or collected an assist in six-straight matches for club and country since his brace of helpers against Elversberg back on 24 October. Taking up his position on the left flank, Nusa did well to beat veteran shot-stopper Karl Darlow with a low drive from the top of the 18-yard box to break the deadlock after the half-time interval. It was Nusa's 10th goal for Norway, and the first for his country since the pair he bagged over the summer across the Atlantic. His pace outwide, competence on the ball, and ability to drive play forward at speed have been at the forefront of Norway's rekindling efforts, and perhaps it's no wonder that Premier League holders and current table-toppers Arsenal have recently been heavily linked with the former Club Brugge standout. Having started alongside the aforementioned Haaland and Ødegaard, as well as Fulham's Oscar Bobb tonight, will Nusa add his name to Norway's Premier League-based ranks come the opening of the January window?

sports.title: 'I was envious': R Ashwin makes honest confession about Ravindra Jadeja
sports.description: Ravichandran Ashwin has offered an interesting account of what made his bowling partnership with Ravindra Jadeja so successful, revealing how he learned to use the left-arm spinner's strengths and limitations to his advantage. Ashwin described Jadeja as an exceptionally gifted cricketer but suggested that the all-rounder initially lacked the instinct to consistently find ways to dismiss batters. The two formed one of the most successful spin combinations in Test cricket, sharing the field in 58 matches and accounting for 587 wickets. While Ashwin claimed 317 of those dismissals, Jadeja contributed 270. According to the former India off-spinner, their success stemmed from understanding each other's contrasting approaches and making the most of them. Speaking on Aakash Chopra's podcast show, Baith & Bol, Ashwin explained that he understood Jadeja's game well enough to help him operate within his strengths rather than push him towards something that did not come naturally to him. “I know his limitations well," Ashwin said. “Very few can bring him out of those limitations. I was one of them. His biggest strength: naturally gifted. If he has a bad day, you just tell him your effort is fine; tomorrow will be better. His action was simple, release point simple, tappa so good—he doesn’t have to think. He didn’t know how to dismiss batsmen—I’m saying he absolutely didn’t know. But his skill to choke batsmen was intertwined with his skill. You can’t sweep him—trajectory is low. You can’t step out—airspeed is good. You can’t play defense without doubting if the ball would remain the same." One aspect of Jadeja's bowling that often came under scrutiny was his reluctance to vary his pace or give the ball more flight, even when the conditions called for it. Ashwin revealed that he had attempted to persuade his spin partner to experiment more, but those efforts often came at the expense of Jadeja's effectiveness and economy. Eventually, Ashwin recognised that Jadeja's ability to keep things tight from one end gave him the freedom to attack from the other. While Jadeja restricted the opposition's scoring opportunities, Ashwin could experiment with different deliveries and concentrate on taking wickets. That combination also made Jadeja more difficult to deal with. Ashwin said developing this understanding gave him even greater appreciation for what Jadeja brought to the team, particularly his remarkable consistency and control. “When I understood that, my respect for Jadeja doubled—what he does is not easy. I have seen many skillful spinners, but the repetitive nature- keeping the ball there at the same speed is very difficult. Spinning the ball at that speed is not easy," he said. sports.description: Saturday marked the first time Wales had beaten New Zealand in 73 years [Getty Images] Welsh rugby fans were "fizzing off their heads" on Saturday night after ending 73 years of hurt against New Zealand in an epic Nations Championship encounter. The match at the Principality Stadium ended 35-28 to the hosts as the All Blacks' run of 34 successive victories against Wales - dating back to 1953 - came to a juddering halt in Cardiff. Wales fans were left stunned by a result that came just a week on from having to grind out a win against Japan. Celebrities were also quick to congratulate the team with Gavin & Stacey star Ruth Jones sharing her disbelief in an Instagram post. Three times Wales led by 14 points, and for the first time in history they scored five tries against New Zealand, but ultimately it was heroic defensive work that denied the visitors. All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie made eight changes from the side that swept past Scotland in their previous Nations Championship game. But the approach backfired spectacularly after a brilliant performance sparked astonishing scenes in Cardiff. Wales scored five tries - a national record against New Zealand - but it was their effort without the ball that ended a 34-game losing streak against the All Blacks. sports.description: USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Connect The Colorado Avalanche will be without superstars Nathan MacKinnon and Cale Makar for an extended period. Avalanche head coach Jared Bednar told reporters in Montreal on Saturday morning that MacKinnon is out for at least a month, while Makar is expected to miss two weeks. Both players suffered lower-body injuries in Ottawa, with the incidents occurring around a minute apart in the second period. To replace MacKinnon in the lineup , Colorado recalled forward Gavin Brindley from the American Hockey League on Saturday. The Denver Post’s Corey Masisak confirmed that Brock Nelson will move up to the top line in MacKinnon’s absence, while Nic Roy will center a line with Gabe Landeskog . Nazem Kadri will center another line. On defense, rookie Alex Gagne will make his NHL debut alongside Brent Burns, who is set to appear in his 1,600th career regular-season game. That likely means Noah Juulsen moves up to play with Brett Kulak, leaving Devon Toews and Sam Malinski together as the top pair. The top power play will also have Toews and Artturi Lehkonen on it. They’ll join Martin Necas, T.J. Hughes, and Kadri, as they did after Thursday’s injuries . MacKinnon is Colorado’s top point producer, recording 10 goals, 20 assists, and 30 points in 20 games this season. Makar, who previously missed a game for the birth of his twin children, has five goals and 23 points in 19 games. This is a rare situation for Colorado. Saturday’s matchup against the Canadiens will mark just the seventh time that both superstars have been unavailable for the same game since Makar made his NHL debut. It’s also the first time since March 2021 that both players will miss the same game outside of occasional late-season rest ahead of the playoffs. Bednar said Makar’s injury is soft tissue-related and that there is no concern it will linger beyond the current recovery timeline. The timing offers the Avalanche at least a little relief. Colorado has just five games scheduled over the next two weeks, meaning Makar could miss a relatively small portion of the schedule if he returns as expected. MacKinnon’s absence, however, is expected to stretch considerably longer. There’s no question that it’s going to be a challenge. sports.title: NFL Rumors: Green Bay Packers Pursued Trade for Starting RB, Balked at Club’s High Asking Price
sports.description: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Green Bay Packers have the worst rushing offense in the NFL this season, ranking last in rushing yards per game (68.2) with the second-lowest yards per carry average (3.0). Hoping to improve things with Josh Jacobs out multiple weeks, general manager Brian Gutekunst reportedly pursued a deal for a new starting running back. According to ESPN ‘s Adam Schefter, Green Bay and the Denver Broncos both inquired with the Tennessee Titans regarding the availability of running back Tony Pollard. Tennessee was open to dealing the 29-year-old running back, who is in a contract year, but the asking price reportedly pushed Green Bay and Denver away. Tony Pollard stats (2026): 595 rushing yards, 6 rushing touchdowns, 4.5 yards per carry The Titans front office made it clear that Pollard wouldn’t be moved for anything less than a third-round pick. From Tennessee’s perspective, Pollard’s recent stretch of success (322 rushing yards and 5.0 yards per carry in last three games) was instrumental in the improved play as of late from quarterback Cam Ward. Unless Green Bay or Denver was willing to overpay for a half season of Pollard, a deal wouldn’t be made. It’s the second running back Green Bay has been connected to in NFL trade rumors. Even before Jacobs’ injury, the Packers reportedly inquired with the Indianapolis Colts regarding All-Pro running back Jonathan Taylor. While he was technically available, Indianapolis wanted a first-round pick for him or multiple Day 2 picks in the 2027 NFL Draft and future draft capital. The Micah Parsons trade leaves Green Bay without a first-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. Gutekunst’s draft capital took another blow this week when the Miami Dolphins placed quarterback Malik Willis on injured reserve. Because he’s now expected to miss at least four games, the projected third-round compensatory pick Green Bay anticipated receiving for Miami signing him will likely now be a fourth-round selection in 2027. Ultimately, Gutekunst just couldn’t justify sacrificing all of his Day 2 picks and additional assets for Taylor nor was he willing to give up a third-round pick for half a season of Pollard. Given that Green Bay’s offensive line has been one of the biggest reasons for the run game’s struggles, that could prove to be the right decision. science.description: The first Aliens: Fireteam Elite was among my favorite Alien video games , and there were a lot of reasons to be excited for a sequel. At Summer Game Fest 2026 , we learned of many smart changes and improvements to the formula, and I was eager to go bug-hunting again. A new campaign, fully reworked classes, and four-player co-op. What could go wrong? Months later, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2's debut has been difficult, mostly due to glaring tech issues. Despite this, it's still a welcome jolt of action for a franchise that's been focusing on making the Xenomorphs scary again in recent years. Alien: Romulus (2024) and Alien: Earth (2025) have reestablished the acid-blooded Xenomorphs as bona fide horror icons, while games like Aliens: Dark Descent bet on tense real-time tactics and squad management; Rogue Incursion spooked VR and non-VR players alike; and we even have Isolation 2 's pure survival horror to look forward to. Rough edges aside, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is a necessary return to mindless shooting and treating the Xenos as a relentless horde, dropping the stalking and slasher-inspired murders in favor of sci-fi shootouts and macho one-liners. It's far from a novel idea — even the original game is only five years old — but a classic for a reason. Another glorious day in the Corps (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) Believe it or not, another colony has fallen prey to the Xenomorphs in Fireteam Elite 2. The familiar setup takes a new team of Colonial Marines to a mining facility on LV-558, where contact has been lost with the first wave of Marines that went in to deal with the threat. This isn't first contact; the Marines are more than used to bug hunts by now, which means there's less exposition to cut through before getting to the Xeno-blasting chaos. The writing certainly won't stun the Academy (and there's definitely too much of it in between missions), but the agility here is appreciated. We've fought these aliens many, many times before. Fireteam Elite 2 is smart enough to sidestep fake tension and just hit the ground running. (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) All the design changes and upgrades reinforce the intent to make the ultimate Aliens action game. Classes have more defined roles and access to better, more destructive sci-fi weapons, and the upgrade to four-player fireteams is welcome when aliens and hostile synths won't stop pouring in. Tired of replaying campaign missions on higher difficulties and with modifiers? Prepare for the worst in this shooter's version of the classic horde mode. At its best, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 understands why James Cameron's masterpiece still holds up. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
science.description: null On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier. The Apollo 12 moonwalkers also performed a lot of moon science. The astronauts picked up 75 pounds of moon rocks. Most of the rocks were basalts that formed from molten lava. These basalts showed the Apollo 12 landing site is more than 3 billion years old. The Apollo 12 astronauts on NASA's second crewed moon landing mission. They are (left to right) are Charles Conrad Jr., Richard F. Gordon Jr., and Alan L. Bean. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered Apollo 12 proved that the Apollo 11 moon landing was not just a one-off stunt while setting the stage for even more ambitious missions. To truly explore the moon and advance our understanding of how our solar system formed, the follow-on Apollo flights needed to be able to land where the geologists had identified as areas of interest. Apollo 12, with its touchdown in proximity to the Surveyor probe, proved this was possible. The Apollo 12 astronauts visited NASA's Surveyor 3 lander and took samples of it back to Earth. (Image credit: NASA) The launch of Apollo 12 also underscored the importance of having a well-prepared Mission Control team, an asset that would be critical to outcome of the next mission, Apollo 13. The ability to recover from a complete electrical short out with the simple call of a through of a switch "SCE to AUX" proved that knowing every detail about how the spacecraft worked was key to a successful program. science.title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
science.description: null Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029. Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky . It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth . The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years , when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse. Jupiter, Mars and Regulus will appear close together on the night of Nov. 15-16. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva.) Both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus , which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun . A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant , formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams. How to measure distances in the night sky using your outstretched hand. science.title: New Scientist readers on how the magazine has shaped their lives
science.description: Have you been reading New Scientist since the start? Getty Images/Westend61 The first issue of New Scientist was published on 22 November 1956, and some of our readers have been with us since the very beginning. We asked subscribers, young and old, to tell us how they first encountered the magazine and how New Scientist has influenced their lives. The volume of responses and the gratitude expressed within them were quite overwhelming. Here are some of our favourites, featuring a spectacular maggot experiment, science-inspired poetry and even a match made on the short-lived New Scientist dating site. Huge thanks to everyone who wrote in. I was interested to see that New Scientist was launched “for all those men and women who are interested in scientific discovery and in its industrial, commercial and social consequences”. At the age of 13, I saved up a shilling from my Saturday morning “jobs” to purchase the first edition on 22 November 1956 and became one of those people interested in scientific discovery. Seventy years later, I remain a subscriber, after a scientific career that took me to many (if not, most!) countries in the world. New Scientist covered things like the opening of Jodrell Bank telescope in 1957. Since that was only about 50 miles (80 kilometres) away, it necessitated a bike ride to see what it really looked like! Peter Hall Advertisement I seem to have been reading New Scientist for the full 70! I do recall my encounter with the first edition: I was at Bec Grammar School in south London in a second-year physics class – it was 1956. The teacher, a genial boffin-type, announced the advent of the new publication and handed out copies – all I remember is its grey (or was it beige?) pages, which I read in a perfunctory way (I was only 12!) little thinking it would follow me through life and around the globe. Robyn Williams I was at Malvern College in England for my O level examinations from 1955 to 1958. My science master at Malvern had recognised my interest in science and technology and he bought the very first issue of New Scientist with his own money. At the next science class, he stood up in front of the whole class and waved the first issue, saying, “Young Inman, a new UK science and technology magazine has been published and here is the first issue for you.” I went on to reach 60 years as a member of the UK Institution of Civil Engineers. Peter Inman 1956 puts me back at school – Fettes College in Edinburgh. The school adopted New Scientist from its first edition and it was available in the library, where senior boys interested in science were recommended to read it. And so began a lifetime of New Scientist – I have been a regular for as long as I can remember and a subscriber for a very long time. I am very grateful to New Scientist for maintaining my interest in all the sciences and new developments, which I am sure has helped me to think laterally and to have a greater understanding of what makes everything tick. Frank Eva

science.title: SpaceX launches Starship on ambitious 22-hour Flight 15 test, but aborts booster 'chopsticks' catch (video)
science.description: null STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX launched the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX 's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch. Following stage separation, Super Heavy reoriented for a planned return to Starbase as Ship powered its way toward low Earth orbit (LEO). SpaceX originally planned to catch Super Heavy with the Starbase launch tower's giant mechanical "chopstick" arms. But it wasn't to be: The company called off the catch attempt and brought the booster down for a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after launch, for reasons that were not immediately clear. A successful catch would have been a significant milestone for SpaceX and its efforts to design Starship as a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle. It would have been the first successful recovery of a Version 3 (V3) Super Heavy , which SpaceX began flying earlier this year. The company previously recovered three of its V1 Super Heavy vehicles and reused two of those in later flights. "We’ve got a nominal orbit insertion, so Starship now in orbit around Earth for the second time ever," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during today's Flight 15 launch webcast. "That’s a really great moment." science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
science.description: null On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona. Mariner 9 worked for one year in orbit. When it ran out of gas, NASA shut it off. But the spacecraft remains one of the most famous Mars voyagers of all time. The Mariner 9 spacecraft, seen here in a NASA model, was the first to orbit Mars in 1971. (Image credit: NASA) Here's why it mattered Mariner 9 cemented its place in space history when it entered into orbit around Mars, the first human-built spacecraft ever to do so. The NASA spacecraft actually beat the Soviet Union's own Mars 2 spacecraft to the Red Planet, even though Mars 2 "had an 11-day head start," NASA said in a mission description . (Mars 2 would go on to be the first human-built craft to impact the surface of Mars when it crashed into the Red Planet.) But it was the science from Mariner 9 that transformed Mars from a mysterious Red Planet into a full world for humans to explore. The Boldest Mars Missions in History The Mariner 9 mission first saw the peak of Olympus Mons on Mars in the midst of a global dust storm in 1971. (Image credit: NASA/JPL) Mariner 9 carried four primary instruments to study Mars, including a camera system for imaging, an ultraviolet spectrometer, an infrared spectrometer and an infrared radiometer. The probe mapped 85% of Mars with those tools during its nearly one-year mission. The Mariner 9 spacecraft discovered 20 giant volcanoes on Mars (including Olympus Mars) and made key observations to map Valles Marineris, which runs 2,500 miles (4,000 kilometers) long acros the Tharsis region and is 120 miles (200 km) wide. "The canyon was named in honor of Mariner 9," NASA said in an overview . In all, Mariner 9 took 7,329 photos of the surface of Mars, mapping the planet down to a resolution of between 1/2-1 mile (1-2 km). It also snapped at least 80 photos of Phobos and Deimos, the two small moons of Mars. By February 1972, Mariner 9's supply of gaseous nitrogen, which it used to feed its attitide control thrusters, had run dry. NASA finally shut down the mission in October 1972. science.title: 60 years ago the Leonid meteor shower produced 144,000 meteors per hour. Could it happen again?
science.description: null This year marks a rather auspicious anniversary for meteor watchers. Sixty years ago , one of the most stupendous Leonid meteor displays lit up the predawn skies over the central and western U.S. So, what will the 2026 Leonids bring us? And what might they bring in the years to come? The Leonid meteor shower is one of the most celebrated of the year's annual displays of "shooting stars." The mere mention of the Leonids usually elicits mental images of a sky filled with shooting stars pouring down through the sky like rain. Such meteor storms have indeed occurred with the Leonids, such as in 1833 and 1966 when meteor rates of tens of thousands per hour were observed. In more recent years, most notably 1999 , 2001 and 2002 , lesser Leonid displays of up to "only" a few thousand meteors per hour took place. Unfortunately, that's not likely to be the case this year. In fact, comparatively speaking, this is going to be a lean year for the Leonids chiefly because of the expected lack of any significant activity. Although the Leonids are one of the most famous of all the annual meteor displays, this year they're not likely to be very productive. It's probable they are going to be rather weak and there probably will be long stretches when not a single Leonid will be seen. I'll explain why in a moment. First, let's find out about this shower's lineage. What causes the Leonids? The Leonids are so named because the shower's radiant point, from where the meteors seem to fan out, is located within the constellation of Leo the Lion, from the backward question mark pattern of stars known as " The Sickle." The meteors are caused by the Tempel-Tuttle comet , which sweeps through the inner solar system every 33⅓ years. Each time the comet passes closest to the sun it leaves a "river of rubble" in its wake: a dense trail of dusty debris. A meteor storm becomes possible if the Earth were to score a direct hit on a fresh dust trail ejected by the comet over the past several centuries. The "lion's share" (no pun intended) of comet dust can be found just ahead and trailing behind Tempel-Tuttle. That comet last swept through the inner solar system in 1998. That's why spectacular meteor showers were seen in 1999, 2001 and 2002, with declining numbers thereafter. The most famous depiction of the 1833 Leonids, actually produced in 1888 for the Adventist book Bible Readings for the Home Circle . The engraving is by Adolf Vollmy based upon an original painting by the Swiss artist Karl Jauslin, that is in turn based on a first-person account of the 1833 storm by a minister, Joseph Harvey Waggoner on his way from Florida to New Orleans. Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. science.title: 100 launches! Rocket Lab sends Earth-observing satellite to orbit on milestone mission (photos)
science.description: null Rocket Lab just hit the century mark. An Electron rocket topped with a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite lifted off from Rocket Lab's New Zealand site on Saturday (Nov. 14) at 12:30 a.m. EST (0530 GMT; 6:30 p.m. local New Zealand time). The mission, which Rocket Lab called "The Mountain God Rises," was a big one: It marked the 100th launch to date for the California-based company. The first stage of Rocket Lab's Electron rocket falls back to Earth during "The Mountain God Rises" mission on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) Rocket Lab launched for the first time in May 2017, sending the brand-new Electron up on a test flight from New Zealand. That effort failed, but Electron bounced back on its second-ever liftoff, delivering several cubesats to low Earth orbit (LEO) in January 2018. In the years since, the 59-foot-tall (18 meters) Electron has become one of the most prolific and reliable rockets in the world, carrying small payloads to the final frontier for a variety of customers. And it hit the century mark on Saturday in record-breaking fashion: No commercially developed rocket has gotten there faster, not even SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9 , according to Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck. "It's an unprecedented milestone for a commercial small-lift orbital rocket, and a threshold rarely crossed in modern spaceflight," Beck said on Monday (Nov. 9), during Rocket Lab's third-quarter earnings call with investors. "But what matters most to us and our customers is that we have achieved a 96% reliability rate across 99 launches." Electron met the moment in style on Saturday morning, thanks to some fancy livery. "Black rocket 🤝 Golden milestone. Electron is all dressed up for launch 100," Rocket Lab said via X on Tuesday (Nov. 10), in a post that shared a photo of the specially painted first stage. Not all of Rocket Lab's missions have gone orbital, it should be noted: A suborbital variant of Electron known as HASTE , which customers use to test technologies in a hypersonic flight environment, has nine missions under its belt to date. The Electron rocket that flew Rocket Lab's 100th mission sported some special livery. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) "The Mountain God Rises" was Rocket Lab's 11th launch to date for the Tokyo-based company iQPS, which is building a constellation of three dozen synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites in LEO. And all went to plan on the mission: Electron's upper "kick stage" deployed a single iQPS spacecraft 357 miles (575 kilometers) above Earth. SAR satellites can see through cloud cover and image our planet at night as well as during the day, offering key advantages over spacecraft that are optimized to view in optical wavelengths. science.title: California's brand-new Air & Space Center, home of the space shuttle Endeavour, opens today
science.description: null LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov. 13). After more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive new wing. For most of us, the biggest draw is its centerpiece: the retired space shuttle Endeavour , sitting upright in launch position, towering at nearly 200 feet (61 meters) tall. "It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time. It's just — it's overwhelming," former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com during a visit to the museum. Reisman flew on two space shuttle missions during his astronaut career, the first of which was on Endeavour. The space shuttle Endeavour. (Image credit: Olivia Hemaratanatorn/Future) "There are people that come from all over the world, and when they come to Los Angeles, they're going to have the opportunity to see it, too," Reisman added. "The exposure it's going to have is just a force multiplier. There are so many people that can have that opportunity to bring their kids here and show them [the shuttle] and have that experience." Entering into this exhibit is an experience in and of itself, as I can personally attest; I was among of group of reporters who got a sneak peek at the new wing on Oct. 28. A video presentation ends in a dramatic reveal: Visitors walk into a space where the enormous shuttle, which flew 25 missions to Earth orbit from 1992 to 2011, feels truly larger than life. The new Endeavour exhibit features a replica launch tower, from which you can look down at the shuttle. (Image credit: Future) There are a number of interactive exhibits around the base of Endeavour, which you can slide down to (though, of course, you can also take the elevator or stairs). From a shuttle landing simulator to a replica of a shuttle cockpit that you can sit in, to shuttle tires and space tech from across decades of spaceflight history, there's an incredible variety of space artifacts to both observe and interact with. As for Endeavour itself: It is open, so you can peer inside to see the robotic arm tucked away among a myriad of handles, straps and electronic gear inside. And you can see the shuttle from underneath all the way to the top. A replica of the space shuttle Endeavour's flight deck. (Image credit: Olivia Hemaratanatorn/Future) You can lie on the floor underneath the shuttle's engines, for example, and then take an elevator up the launch tower to come face-to-face with Endeavour's nose. There's even a transparent floor at the top that allows you to stand above the shuttle (though if you have a fear of heights, this might not be for you). science.title: Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight
science.description: null Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars. In fact, you're likely to catch their collective brightness in your peripheral vision every time you go outside and look up. But every November the Pleiades remind me that naked-eye observing isn't as simple as opening the back door and looking up. How many Pleiades I can see can change depending on what I do during the next 10 minutes. What's happening and when to look You can easily see the Pleiades as a bright misty patch in your peripheral vision during winter. (Image credit: Haitong Yu via Getty Images) The Pleiades, also known as Messier 45 (M45) or the "Seven Sisters," are an open star cluster in Taurus. They're one of the closest clusters to the solar system and some of the youngest stars you can see with the naked eye — just 100 million years old. They're basically newborns. In mid-November, they rise in the east in the early evening and climb higher as the night progresses, making this an excellent time to get acquainted with them. Look east after dark for a tiny, compact group of stars. If you know Orion, which rises later, the Pleiades are above and to the right of it from mid-northern latitudes. Nearby you'll also find orange Aldebaran and the much broader V-shaped Hyades cluster. The Hyades are closer to the sun , but their stars are about 625 million years old. The name "Seven Sisters" creates an immediate observational trap: people assume they're supposed to see seven stars. That's not necessarily true. In fact, six is a common naked-eye result under decently dark conditions (note that the shape of the six brightest is like a mini Big Dipper /Plough), while people with sharp eyesight under darker skies may see more. The cluster itself contains about 1,000 stars. The number you personally distinguish depends on eyesight, sky brightness, atmospheric conditions and how well your eyes have adapted to darkness. That makes M45 much more interesting to me than a simple tick-box target. So tonight, don't just find the Pleiades — count them. science.title: 'Martian Isolation' is an upcoming sci-fi survival horror game that looks like 'The Martian' and 'Event Horizon' had a horrific child
science.description: null "Martian Isolation" is an upcoming single-player, first-person survival horror game that's just been revealed with a suitably creepy launch trailer. And yes, it does look an awful lot like " The Martian ," doesn't it? There's a lot of survival gameplay on display here that mirrors Mark Watney's tale of survival on the Red Planet, as your stranded protagonist is forced to explore the Martian surface to acquire resources, grow plants, and repair their base. That comparison to Andy Weir's sci-fi masterpiece does fall away as you get further into the trailer, though, when the horror part of the game's description comes into play: Flickering lights, creepy figures stalking the halls of your Martian habitat, and blood dripping from the walls. Oh yeah, that's some good creepy sci-fi horror right there. It's giving " Event Horizon ", and that's always getting a thumbs-up from me. There's no release date scheduled at this time, with the 'Martian Isolation' Steam page simply listing it as "coming soon," though the YouTube trailer description does say it "will be available on Steam in 2027". You can't pre-order yet, but if this looks like your jam, you can add it to your wishlist. Beyond that, we know shockingly little about this title. It's the debut game from Golden Milestone Studio, but there's very little information out there beyond a name. The latest blog post on the game's Steam page says that they're a "small team," but what we've seen so far is encouraging. There seems to be a pronounced split between the survival and horror elements of the game along the day/night cycle. Daytime sees you exploring the Martian surface, smashing rocks, cleaning solar panels, and doing sick jumps on a quad bike. The psychological torment only begins once the sun goes down (they mostly come out at night … mostly), as your character starts encountering cosmic horrors and weird naked zombie men. Mars rover, nice. Golden Milestone Studio Spacesuits, check. Golden Milestone Studio Crafting, of course. Golden Milestone Studio OH SWEET JESUS! Get it away, get it away. Golden Milestone Studio OK, we're good. Mining, cool. Golden Milestone Studio Riding a quad bike on Mars, yes please. Golden Milestone Studio Growing potatoes on Mars, just like that guy in the movie. Golden Milestone Studio Opening a box with power tools, seems excessive but sure. Golden Milestone Studio NOPE! Nope, nope, nope, I'm out! Golden Milestone Studio Are they hallucinations, or is there some malevolent presence hiding in the blood-red sands of Mars ? I'm always looking for new ways to shatter my psyche and possibly soil my pants, so I'll be keeping a close eye on this one. In the meantime, I do need to get back and finish " Routine ." I left my character hiding under a desk months ago, and I haven't been brave enough to go back. As Mama always said, you can't have any Martian horror until you finish your lunar horror first.

science.title: Astronomers trace mystery radio signals back to cosmic odd couple of white dwarf and sun-like star
science.description: null Astronomers have traced a mysterious radio signal back to a cosmic odd couple comprised of a dead star, a white dwarf, and its stellar companion, a sun-like star. The white dwarf in the newly discovered system, designated GPM J071507−114153 and located around 5,000 light-years away, spins once every eight minutes, sending out radio pulses. These radio pulses have been seen from binary systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars before, but rarely from a system like GPM J071507−114153. GPM J071507−114153 belongs to a class of celestial objects called long-period transients (LPTs) known to produce radio signals that switch on and off over intervals of minutes or hours. Around a dozen LPTs have been detected since the team behind this research found the first in 2021. Several previously discovered LPT systems contain a white dwarf and a companion star, but it has been unclear which of the two stars was generating the radio pulses. That means the discovery of GPM J071507−114153 and finding that the pulses come from close to the white dwarf could be a significant step toward understanding the nature of LPTs. The unusual system consists of a small and highly energetic white dwarf pulsar, orbiting a much larger star similar to our sun. (Image credit: ICRAR) "This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion," team leader and commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKA), Sam McSweeney, said in a statement . "So we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself." The pulses seen by the team also allowed them to detect stellar flares erupting on the sun-like star. "As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence,' which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface," team member Natasha Hurley-Walker of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR), Curtin University, Australia, said. "It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away." South Africa’s MeerKAT telescope. (Image credit: South African Radio Astronomy Observatory (SARAO)) Hurley-Walker and the team at ICRAR have been at the cutting edge of rare star systems like this. "We detected this system in a large survey using the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia," Hurley-Walker said. science.title: Gemini Astronaut Photos Inspired Early Earth Observation Program
science.description: NASA astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. captured this image of the area surrounding the Red Sea and Nile river valley on November 14, 1966, during their four-day mission in space. Gemini XII was the final flight of NASA’s Gemini Program. NASA Astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. orbited Earth from November 11 to 15, 1966, on Gemini XII , the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program. In addition to successfully completing rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks, procedures vital to sending American astronauts to the Moon, the crew was also spurring the development of a different field of exploration, observing Earth from space. The photos taken by Lovell, Aldrin, and other Gemini astronauts demonstrated the value of orbital imagery for studying Earth’s surface. Their images helped scientists make the case for a dedicated Earth observation satellite program. One of strongest advocates for accelerating the use of Earth-observing satellites was William T. Pecora, the director of the United States Geological Survey from 1965 to 1971. In a 1969 statement, Pecora noted that the Earth Resources Observation Satellite (EROS) program he championed, and which later paved the way for Landsat , was “conceived in 1966 largely as a direct result of the demonstrated utility of Mercury and Gemini orbital photography to Earth resource studies.” For more than five decades, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites have provided invaluable data used around the world to monitor crops, wildfires, flooding, vegetation health, land use, and countless other changes to our planet.
